name: Boiling point
seoTitle: Boiling point Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Boiling point: work out boiling point (State 2) from the pressure. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Boiling point calculator returns boiling point (State 2) from the 4 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It suits a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Boiling point calculator work?
sections.html:
The Boiling point calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports boiling point (State 2) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the substance); then you type in the pressure (State 1) and the pressure (State 2).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 9 options, such as water, acetone and ammonia. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Show heat of vaporization”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in hectopascals. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in hectopascals. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Boiling point calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Boiling point=(50000 × heat of vaporization × boiling point ÷ (50000 × heat of vaporization + 415723 × boiling point × the natural log of (pressure ÷ pressure)))
Pressure=(pressure)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Substance set to Water, Heat of vaporization = 10 kJ, Pressure = 10 hPa and Boiling point = 10 °C. Working through the relationship above gives Pressure = 10 hPa and Boiling point = 10 °C.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Pressure = 10 hPa and Boiling point = 10 °C should be roughly the size you expected from Substance set to Water and Heat of vaporization = 10 kJ.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Energy, opening in kilojoules
  • Pressure, opening in hectopascals
  • Pressure, opening in hectopascals
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Pressure, opening in hectopascals
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Boiling point calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the pressure — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Boiling point calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns boiling point (State 2), derived from the pressure. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Boiling point calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pressure, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter heat of vaporization in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Heat of vaporization opens in kilojoules and the chip beside it offers 33 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Pressure = 10 hPa. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Boiling point calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
